Generative Monte Carlo Particle Transport

A standard Monte Carlo transport baseline in 2D, a single-cell transmission dataset built from it, and a conditional flow-matching model that samples cell exit states directly — replacing the scattering random walk with one network call. Every number below was produced by the code described here.

01What we are building

Standard Monte Carlo transport costs more as a cell gets optically thicker, because it must resolve every scattering event inside it. The paper's claim is that this cost can be made constant: train a generative model to sample a particle's exit state from a cell directly, and the random walk inside never has to happen.

A particle entering a mesh cell scatters some number of times and eventually leaves. Standard Monte Carlo simulates each of those collisions. In a cell that is L mean free paths across, that is O(L) work per crossing — we measure this directly in §2, and it is exactly linear.

Generative Monte Carlo replaces that loop with one draw from a learned conditional distribution. Given the state the particle entered with, sample where it comes out, which way it is going, and how far it travelled. One network call, independent of optical thickness.

Scope of this document

Everything here was built and measured. Where the paper leaves something unspecified, the choice made is marked ours and justified. Where a claim was verified numerically, the check is shown. Section 9 lists what is not established, which matters as much as what is.

02The Monte Carlo baseline

Two independent solvers share the physics but not the code: a full-domain transport solver that produces benchmark flux fields, and a single-cell walk that produces training data and the cost measurements.

Physics

Steady-state, monoenergetic linear Boltzmann transport on a 2D Cartesian mesh with isotropic scattering. Three choices define the implementation:

  • 2D geometry, 3D directions. Positions are (x, y); directions live on the full unit sphere. A sampled flight ds is the true 3D path length, and the position advances by ox·ds, oy·ds with z ignored by translational invariance. This is the standard "2D XY" treatment, and it is what makes the mean-chord identity in the validation below come out as L rather than πL/4.
  • Implicit capture. Collision distances are sampled from the scattering cross section only, ds = −ln ξ / σ_s, and weight is attenuated continuously along every track segment by exp(−σ_a·ds).
  • Track-length flux estimator. Each segment deposits Δw / (V·σ_a) with Δw = w(1 − e^{−σ_a ds}), reducing to w·ds/V as σ_a → 0. Tallies are normalised per source particle.

Histories end when the particle leaves the domain or its weight falls below 1e-12. There is no Russian roulette, matching the paper.

Validation against analytic results

Before trusting any of it, both branches of the estimator were checked against results that require no tuning.

Verified · pure scattering

Dirac invariance. For a convex, purely scattering body under cosine-law surface illumination, the mean total track length equals the mean chord 4V/S, independent of σ_s. For an infinite square prism of side A, that is exactly A.

Measured on a 2 cm cell: 2.0010, 1.9969, 1.9931, 2.0023 cm at σ_s = 0.5, 1, 5, 20 — a 40× range of cross section, all within 0.35% of the exact 2.0000.

Verified · with absorption

Total path in an absorbing medium. Every source particle is eventually absorbed, so its expected total track length is exactly 1/σ_a. On a domain large enough that leakage is negligible:

σ_a=1.0 → 1.00000  ·  σ_a=0.5 → 2.00000  ·  σ_a=2.0 → 0.50000 — exact to five decimals.

The exactness is not luck. With implicit capture the per-particle deposit telescopes: Σ w(1−e^{−σ_a ds})/σ_a = (w_initial − w_final)/σ_a. Each particle contributes 1/σ_a deterministically, so the estimator has zero variance for this quantity — which makes it a sharp test of the weight bookkeeping.

Cost scaling — the premise of the whole method

The single-cell walk was timed across five decades of optical thickness. The mean number of scattering events per particle comes out linear in L, to sub-percent:

Cell side L (mfp)13.161031.61003161000
Mean scatters / particle1.03.210.031.6100.7318.81016.6

This is the same mean-chord result seen from the other side: collisions occur once per mean free path, so ⟨k⟩ = ⟨s⟩ = L. It is simultaneously a validation of the walk and a statement of the problem — cost grows without bound as cells get thicker, and GMC's promise is to flatten it.

Statistical convergence

The cell-averaged standard deviation of the scalar flux was measured for both benchmarks at eight particle counts, five independent runs each (Eq. 12 in the paper).

03Geometry

Two benchmarks. The lattice is the one the dataset is built from, so its construction is given as a rule rather than a coordinate list — that is what lets it scale to any size.

The lattice

A 7×7 cm domain holding a 5×5 grid of 1 cm cells on [1,6]², with a 1 cm background margin. Background is σ_s = 1, σ_a = 0; absorber blocks are σ_s = 0.5, σ_a = 9.5. An isotropic volumetric source fills the centre cell. Mesh is 112×112.

The paper's 11 absorber blocks were originally a hard-coded list. Encoding the rule instead generalises the geometry to any odd lattice size K:

cells = {(i,j) : 1 ≤ i,j ≤ K,  (i+j) even}   # even-parity checkerboard
cells -= {(c,c)}                             # centre cell holds the source
cells -= {(c,j) : j ≥ c}                     # chimney: clear the column above

Blocks are two corner points

A block carries three representations, each doing one job. An integer index (i,j); a physical box (x₀,y₀,x₁,y₁) from x₀ = border + (i−1)·pitch; and a set of mesh cells, assigned by testing whether each cell centre lies strictly inside the box.

With 16 mesh cells per pitch, block edges land exactly on mesh cell edges while centres sit at odd multiples of dx/2 — so the strict inequality is never ambiguous and each block covers exactly 16×16 = 256 mesh cells. No staircase, no partial materials. Cross sections are not part of the shape: the box selects which cells, the material says what value goes in them, which is why varying materials in the dataset required no geometry changes.

The hohlraum

A 1.3×1.3 cm linearised hohlraum with a left-boundary source and four materials: black walls (50/50), a red stripe (σ_s=95, σ_a=5), a green frame (90/10) and a blue absorber (5/95). Its role here is a second validation target with very different physics — a boundary source instead of volumetric, and 10 decades of dynamic range.

04Assumptions resolved from the paper

The paper specifies the boundary model precisely and the internal model loosely. Its architecture supplementary (S.1–S.3) is not public, so every network-level decision here is ours.

Not in the paper

The internal model's conditioning vector has no equation, no symbol list — only a sentence stating that ξ_in becomes "the two-dimensional internal position for the source model". Its birth direction is never mentioned as an input at all. Any statement of its full input set, including ours, is reconstruction.

05The dataset

3,145,728single-cell transmissions
16optical sizes, 0.025–20 mfp
4,096entry states per size
~6 sto regenerate, deterministic

One record is one particle entering a cell, walking, and leaving. The lattice determines which cells are worth sampling; no lattice is ever meshed or solved.

Why the parameter axes collapse

The sweep covers lattice size K ∈ {3,5,7,9,11}, pitch ∈ {0.25,0.5,1,2,4} cm, and three material sets — 150 distinct cell types. These reduce to 16 distinct problems, for two reasons that are worth stating precisely because they are easy to get wrong:

  • Pitch and σ_s are not independent. The walk is pure scattering with σ_s = 1 in optical units, so a cell enters only through the product W̃ = pitch × σ_s. Sweeping either sweeps the same axis.
  • K does not change any single-cell distribution. A K=3 and a K=11 lattice with the same pitch and materials contain identical cells. K enters only through composition — how many cells of each kind a lattice holds — which is written to a companion table so records can be reweighted per lattice size.

Deduplicating on W̃ means no compute is spent regenerating the same distribution twice. It also means a record cannot carry provenance: W̃ = 0.5 arises both from the paper absorber (σ_s=0.5, σ_a=9.5, pitch 1) and from background at half pitch (σ_s=1, σ_a=0). Records are therefore keyed by W̃ alone, with the composition table as the authoritative join.

Schema

FieldRoleMeaning
Wconditioningcell optical size, mfp (square, so H = W)
y0conditioningentry height as a fraction of H, ∈ [0,1]
oxi, oyiconditioningentry direction as a point on the unit disk, oxi > 0
ptargetexit perimeter coordinate ∈ [0, 4W), counter-clockwise from origin
oxo, oyo, ozotargetexit direction cosines, unit norm

kdiagnosticscattering events; k = 0 identifies the uncollided branch exactly

Sampling design: coverage beats precision

The record count is fixed by n_cond × per_cond, but the split changes what the data is good for. Few entry states with many samples each resolves the conditional distribution precisely at a handful of points; many entry states with fewer samples covers the conditioning space densely. A conditional generative model needs the latter.

The difference is measurable at identical cost:

SplitEntry states / W̃Effective sample sizeReweighted ⟨s⟩ error (median / max)
192 × 1024192674.8% / 14.2%
4096 × 48409610581.3% / 3.0%

It also fixes a visible artefact: at small W̃ most particles cross uncollided, so their exit direction is their entry direction. With only 192 entry states that population renders as 192 delta spikes instead of a distribution.

Two defects found and fixed

Both were caught by inspecting field ranges rather than by any test, which is worth recording.

Fixed · Ω_z sign bias

The conditioned entry mode took only the positive root oz = +√(1−ox²−oy²). The sign genuinely cannot affect the trajectory — the walk advances x,y by (ox,oy) alone — but an uncollided particle carries its entry Ω_z straight to the exit, and Ω_z is a recorded target. At W̃=0.025, where 97% never scatter, ⟨Ω_z⟩ came out +0.66 instead of 0. Both roots are now sampled.

Fixed · meaningless provenance

Records carried (K, pitch, σ_s, σ_a) copied from an arbitrary representative of each deduplicated W̃. K was constant at 3 for all 3.1M rows, and σ_a was actively misleading. Records are now keyed by W̃ only. The composition table was separately triple-counting background cells, since all three material sets share a background; deduplicated, counts now satisfy background + absorber = K².

06Model architecture

A conditional flow-matching model. It learns a velocity field that transports Gaussian noise into the exit-state distribution, conditioned on the entry state.

The objective

Flow matching trains a velocity field v_θ(x, t, c) to carry a sample from noise at t=0 to data at t=1. With the optimal-transport (rectified) path the training pair is trivially constructed:

z ~ N(0, I)          t ~ U(0, 1)
x_t = (1 − t)·z + t·y              # straight-line interpolation
ẋ_t = y − z                        # its constant velocity

L(θ) = 𝔼 ‖ v_θ(x_t, t, c) − (y − z) ‖²

No simulation during training and no likelihood — just a regression onto a known velocity. At inference the ODE dx/dt = v_θ(x,t,c) is integrated from noise to a sample.

Reading the loss

This loss has a nonzero irreducible floor. Given (x_t, t, c) the target y − z is still random, so the best possible predictor is its conditional mean and the residual variance never vanishes. The absolute loss value therefore says almost nothing about sample quality — only the train/val gap is informative. Judge the model by §8, not by the loss.

Encodings

VectorComponentsDim
Conditioning clog W̃, log H̃, 2ξ − 1, Ω_x,in, Ω_y,in5
Target ycos(2πp/4W̃), sin(2πp/4W̃), Ω_x, Ω_y, Ω_z, log(s/W̃)6

Both are standardised per component after encoding, so the flow's Gaussian prior sees O(1) coordinates everywhere; the statistics ship with the checkpoint and are inverted before decoding. H̃ gets its own slot even though the current data is square — the paper conditions on both independently, and this keeps the interface ready for rectangular data without an architecture change.

The velocity field

Sampling

The path-length clamp deserves a note: the decoded exit point implies a hard geometric lower bound on s — a particle cannot travel less than the straight-line distance from entry to exit. The network does not know this, so it is enforced after decoding.

07Training

Preprocessing

Four transforms are mandatory, all derivable from existing columns:

  1. Encode p. Divide by 4W̃ (its range depends on cell size), then map to (cos, sin) — the coordinate is a circle and a raw scalar creates a false seam.
  2. Rescale s. log(s/W̃), not log s.
  3. Log-scale W̃. It spans 0.025 to 20; linear scaling makes the network nearly blind to thin cells.
  4. Split by entry condition, never by row.
The split fails silently

Each entry condition contributes 48 rows with identical conditioning. A random row-wise split puts the same condition in both train and validation — the model has partly memorised, the validation loss looks excellent, and nothing crashes. Splitting on the 62,240 distinct conditions instead gives 0 overlap, verified.

Pre-training verification

Three checks were run before spending compute, because each is far cheaper to debug before a training run than after one.

CheckResult
Perimeter encode → decode round-tripmax circular error 1.1e-05; all decoded points on the cell boundary pass
k = 0 rows are truly uncollidedΩ_exit = Ω_in exact; s = chord to median 3.5e-08 pass
Uncollided fraction vs analytic ⟨e^{−d}⟩0.4832 vs 0.4834 pass
Condition overlap between train and val0 of 62,240 pass

Configuration

ParameterValueNote

Batches are drawn with replacement rather than by shuffled epochs. In flow matching, revisiting a row is not redundant: each draw gets a fresh t and fresh noise z, so the row supplies only the endpoint while the training example is generated around it.

08Results

Evaluated against Monte Carlo at entry conditions the model has never seen — the reference set uses an independently seeded draw of entry states, so this tests conditional generalisation, not recall.

How to read the numbers

Each quantity is scored by Wasserstein-1 distance against a matched-size MC-vs-MC floor: split the reference samples in half and measure the distance Monte Carlo gets against itself. That is pure statistical noise, and it is the best any sampler could achieve. Ratio to the floor is the verdict — near 1.0 means indistinguishable from MC.

A bug worth recording

The first run of this evaluation showed the model beating the floor in all nine comparisons — impossible if the comparison were fair. The floor was computed from m/2 vs m/2 samples while the model was scored on 1024 vs m. Since W1 between finite samples shrinks like 1/√n, the floor was inflated by ≈√2 — and the observed ratios clustered at 1.29–1.55, right on √2. The corrected version scores both comparisons at identical sample sizes. Everything below is post-fix.

log₁₀ s0.04750.04571.04
perimeter p/4W̃0.02460.02560.96
2.5exit angle Ω_x0.04180.04320.97
log₁₀ s0.04410.04401.00
perimeter p/4W̃0.01640.01830.90
10exit angle Ω_x0.02890.03320.87
log₁₀ s0.05680.05551.02
perimeter p/4W̃0.01060.01170.91

All nine ratios fall in 0.85–1.04. By the criteria set before the run, that is the top band: statistically indistinguishable from Monte Carlo at this sample size, across a 20× range of optical thickness. Ratios slightly below 1.0 are ordinary estimator noise in a median over 48 conditions — unlike the earlier √2 artefact, they are not systematic.

Agreement to ≤0.017 absolute everywhere. The one consistent soft spot is right — the model slightly under-produces forward transmission at thin cells.

What the figure shows that the numbers hide

This is why both were needed. In the W̃=0.5 perimeter panel, the model spikes at p/4W̃ = 0.75 — reaching ~2.15 against MC's ~1.5 — and sits low across 0.80–0.95. It is piling mass onto the top-left corner that belongs spread along the left face.

The W1 for that panel is 0.0246, below the floor. Wasserstein-1 is an integral measure and averages a local defect away. A visible shape error can coexist with an excellent score, and reporting only the table would have concealed it.

The same row shows the model's path-length left tail running above MC between −2.5 and −0.5: it over-produces short paths at thin cells. Both artefacts shrink with W̃ and are essentially gone by W̃=10.

Why thin cells are the weak spot

Two compounding causes, both predicted in advance. Fewest training samples — after removing the uncollided branch, W̃=0.5 retains far fewer rows than W̃=10, while generation was flat at 196,608 per size. And sharpest structure — thin cells have the most pronounced corner features, since particles exit close to where they entered. The fix is W̃-dependent sample allocation, and regeneration costs ~6 seconds.

09Conclusions

What was established

  • A Monte Carlo transport baseline that reproduces two analytic invariants — mean chord to 0.35% across a 40× cross-section range, and total absorbed path length exactly to five decimals.
  • Standard MC cost is exactly linear in optical thickness, ⟨k⟩ = W̃ from 0.01 to 1000 mfp. This is the premise GMC exists to defeat, measured rather than assumed.
  • A size-parameterised lattice generator that reproduces the paper's geometry bit-for-bit and extends to any odd K.
  • A 3.15M-record single-cell dataset, with two defects found and fixed before use.
  • A conditional flow-matching sampler whose exit-state marginals are statistically indistinguishable from Monte Carlo at unseen entry conditions, across a 20× range of optical thickness.

What is not established

Read this before citing the result

The joint distribution is untested. §8 checks exit angle, path length and position separately. The transport solver uses (p, Ω, s) together, and matching marginals does not guarantee matching correlations. Marginal agreement is necessary, not sufficient.

No end-to-end test. The sampler has not been chained through a full transport solve. Errors could accumulate over the ~10 crossings a typical history makes.

No speed claim. The O(1) advantage is architectural, not yet measured against the MC baseline in a like-for-like setting.

The σ̄ offset is unexplained. Our convergence sits ~2× below the paper's curves. Any variance comparison between GMC and MC rests on this number.

Square cells, discrete W̃. The dataset has H = W throughout and only 16 optical sizes, where the paper draws from a continuous distribution. Adequate for the lattice; not a faithful reproduction.

Next steps, in order

  1. End-to-end lattice test. Swap the sampler into the transport solver, compare the flux field against the MC reference. This exercises the joint distribution and error accumulation at once — the decisive test.
  2. W̃-dependent sample allocation. Fixes the thin-cell artefacts. Six seconds of regeneration.
  3. Continuous W̃ and rectangular cells. Required for anything claiming to reproduce the paper.
  4. Root-cause the σ̄ offset.

A note on the internal model

The paper specifies two networks — boundary and internal. We built only the boundary model, deliberately: the hohlraum invokes the internal model zero times (its source is on the boundary) and the lattice needs it for one event per particle history against 5–20 boundary crossings. Running analog Monte Carlo for the source cell costs O(W̃) once per history, amortised over many O(1) crossings, and eliminates an entire second model with its own dataset and failure modes.

If a unified model is wanted later, the promising formulation is depth conditioning: trace any particle backwards along −Ω to the boundary point B it came from, and condition on the normalised depth u it has already travelled. Boundary entry is u = 0; internal birth is u > 0. This is exact by memorylessness, makes the direction domain uniform (every particle is inward-moving relative to its own entry face), and — unlike naive (x₀, y₀) conditioning — separates "just arrived" from "about to leave" instead of collapsing them onto the same coordinate. The paper does not discuss combining the models at all, so this remains open ground.

10Reproduction

Every number in this document comes from these commands. Data generation and training are deterministic given the seeds shown.

Environment

pip install numpy numba matplotlib torch
# GPU optional — the trainer auto-detects cuda/mps and falls back to cpu

1 — Monte Carlo benchmarks

python scripts/fig2b_singlecell.py       # single-cell exit statistics
python scripts/fig3_benchmarks.py        # lattice + hohlraum flux and lineouts
python scripts/fig4a_convergence.py      # 1/sqrt(N) convergence, ~5 min
python scripts/fig4b_scaling.py          # cost vs optical thickness, ~1 min
python scripts/lattice_explore.py --k 3 5 7 9

2 — Datasets

# training set: dense conditioning coverage
python scripts/make_lattice_dataset.py \
    --n-cond 4096 --per-cond 48 --seed 777 \
    --out data/lattice_singlecell_coverage.npz

# evaluation set: independent seed, held-out entry conditions
python scripts/make_lattice_dataset.py
Keep the seeds apart

Never train on the evaluation file, and if you regenerate with different flags keep the two sets on different seeds — otherwise the "unseen conditions" property breaks silently and the results in §8 stop meaning anything.

3 — Train

python scripts/train_boundary_model.py
# → models/boundary_v1/{model.pt, normalizers.json, loss_curve.png, train_log.txt}
# flags: --steps --batch --width --depth --lr --device --out

4 — Evaluate

python scripts/eval_boundary_model.py
# → figures/gmc_boundary_eval.png + the W1 table of §8

5 — Use the sampler

from gmc import VelocityField, GMCBoundarySampler
from gmc.data import load_normalizers
import torch

state = torch.load("models/boundary_v1/model.pt", weights_only=True)
cfg   = state["config"]
model = VelocityField(**{k: cfg[k] for k in ("x_dim","c_dim","width","depth")})
model.load_state_dict(state["ema"])          # always sample from EMA weights
ynorm, cnorm, _ = load_normalizers("models/boundary_v1/normalizers.json")

sampler = GMCBoundarySampler(model, ynorm, cnorm)
out = sampler.sample(W=2.0, H=2.0, xi=0.5, oxi=0.8, oyi=0.1, seed=1)
# out["p"], out["dir"], out["s"], out["face"], out["uncollided"]
